summary:
Annuality and perenniality are flexible life-history strategies that shift across evolutionary and population timescales; neither is always ancestral. Annuals make up about 6% of plant species and 15% of herbaceous species, and evolved independently in more than 120 plant families. They are favored where adult mortality exceeds seedling survival, including hot, dry, disturbed, or highly variable environments. Perennials are more likely to persist where adult survival is high.

The strategies involve trade-offs between reproduction and continued growth. Annuals generally allocate more to seeds and reproduce once; most perennials reproduce repeatedly and persist through living plants or clonal growth. These patterns have exceptions, and annuality can be associated with self-fertilization, while perenniality is often linked to outcrossing. Longer generation times also generally make perennial lineages evolve more slowly at the molecular level.

Perennial crops can reduce soil erosion, conserve water and nutrients, and store more carbon than annual crops. Yet high-yield perennial grain crops remain uncommon, partly because perennials may take longer to produce and face growth trade-offs. Researchers are developing crops such as perennial wheat.
